source_construct: blurhash.encode over the image file that PIL re-encoded
target_translation: Decode the upload, apply its EXIF orientation as exif_transpose does, and rebuild the image in the same mode without metadata, as Image.new(mode) + putdata does. For palette (P) images that drops the palette: Pillow's default grayscale palette applies (index i becomes (i,i,i)), and transparency and ICC data go too: BUG(port), reproduced. Store the transposed width and height. Re-encode in the same format (JPEG at quality 75, as Pillow's default), and the 740-pixel WebP thumbnail. Compute the blurhash (4x3) from the re-encoded file after an RGB conversion (alpha dropped, not composited), with an encoder that matches the woltapp C algorithm. For lossless formats the pixels and the blurhash must be exact. For JPEG and WebP the bytes and the blurhash may differ within ADR 0022's thresholds. EXIF must never be stored.

source_construct: dateutil isoparse(...).astimezone(timezone.utc)
target_translation: Support the formats that the callers receive, not all of isoparse (owner decision). Callers and their inputs: (1) remote ActivityPub published, created and endTime (ap_object.py:54, 56, 250; boxes.py:1908, 2380, 2587): RFC 3339 date-times with T, an optional fraction of any length (Mastodon and Misskey send milliseconds, Pleroma microseconds), and Z or ±HH:MM (the original sends Z; some servers +00:00). (2) mf2 dt-published from webmention source pages (facepile.py:149), as mf2py normalizes it: YYYY-MM-DD, a T or a space, an hour of one or two digits, :MM, optional :SS, and an optional zone Z, ±H:MM, ±HH:MM, ±HHMM or ±HH; a value that mf2py doesn't match passes through unchanged, and the common one is a date only (YYYY-MM-DD, midnight). Truncate fractions to 6 digits; a value without a zone is UTC (the deployment's local time). A value outside these forms returns an error, which takes the path that the Python exception takes at that call site. migration/inventory documents this list for the implementer of internal/datetime.

source_construct: async with async_session() around the whole worker loop (one session for the worker's life, expire_on_commit=False)
target_translation: One *database.Session for the worker goroutine's life. The loop itself never commits: the commit and rollback points are inside each message's processing, and the Go code keeps them there (two commits per incoming message, one per outgoing message, rollback on failure). The Go session has no identity map, so each load reads the database's current values. The original can instead return an object cached from an earlier message, with old values; whether it does depends on Python's garbage collector (weak references in SQLAlchemy's identity map). Always reading current values is one of the original's own outcomes, so no BUG(port) marker.
